descriptors.title: Daily and seasonal changes
descriptors.description: describe daily and seasonal changes in the environment and explore how these changes affect everyday life

nodes.label: The environment changes daily and across seasons
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe observable daily changes (weather, temperature, daylight) and identify seasonal patterns across the year.
criteria: Describes at least two observable daily changes in the environment
Names at least two seasons and describes one observable environmental change for each

nodes.label: Daily and seasonal changes affect everyday life
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how daily weather and seasonal changes affect decisions people make and how plants and animals respond to these changes.
criteria: Describes at least one way daily weather change affects a human decision
Describes at least one way seasonal change affects a plant or animal

descriptors.title: Earth in the solar system
descriptors.description: recognise Earth is a planet in the solar system and identify patterns in the changing position of the sun, moon, planets and stars in the sky

nodes.label: Earth is a planet in the solar system
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe Earth as a planet in the solar system, name other planets and the sun, and describe the shape of Earth using images from space.
criteria: Names Earth as a planet in the solar system and identifies at least two other planets
Describes the shape of Earth using evidence from space images

nodes.label: Celestial objects show observable patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe patterns in the changing position of the sun across a day and the changing appearance of the moon across a month, and use these patterns to make predictions.
criteria: Describes the pattern of the sun's movement across a day (direction and shadow change)
Describes the pattern of moon shape change across a month and makes one prediction based on this pattern

descriptors.title: Sound
descriptors.description: explore different actions to make sounds and how to make a variety of sounds, and recognise that sound energy causes objects to vibrate

nodes.label: Sound is produced by different actions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe different actions that produce sound, classify instruments or objects by the action used to produce their sound, and explain that all sound production involves some form of action on an object.
criteria: Names at least four different actions that produce sound with an example of each
Classifies at least three instruments or objects by the action used to produce their sound

nodes.label: Sound energy causes objects to vibrate
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that sound energy causes objects to vibrate, observe and describe vibrations produced by sound-making objects, and connect the speed or strength of vibration to sound properties.
criteria: Describes vibrations in a named sound-making object
Explains that the object vibrates because of sound energy

descriptors.title: Physical changes to materials
descriptors.description: recognise that materials can be changed physically without changing their material composition and explore the effect of different actions on materials including bending, twisting, stretching and breaking into smaller pieces

nodes.label: Physical changes alter shape without changing composition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that physically changing a material (bending, twisting, stretching, breaking) changes its shape or size but not what it is made of.
criteria: Applies at least two physical changes to a material and names each action
Explains that the material is still the same substance after a physical change — only its shape or size has changed

nodes.label: Different actions affect materials differently
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore and describe how different physical actions affect different materials and explain how physical changes can be purposeful.
criteria: Compares how the same physical action affects two different materials
Describes at least one physical change that is purposeful — explaining why the change is useful

descriptors.title: Life cycles
descriptors.description: compare characteristics of living and non-living things and examine the differences between the life cycles of plants and animals

nodes.label: Living, once living and non-living things have distinct characteristics
nodes.checkpoint: Students can classify objects as living, once living or non-living and explain their reasoning using observable characteristics (growth, reproduction, response to environment, need for nutrients).
criteria: Classifies at least five objects as living, once living or non-living with characteristic-based reasoning
Correctly classifies at least one ambiguous case (e.g. seed, dead leaf, fire) with explanation

nodes.label: Life cycles describe stages of growth and change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the life cycle of a named plant and a named animal, identifying the stages in sequence and explaining what changes occur at each stage.
criteria: Names the stages of one plant and one animal life cycle in sequence
Describes the key change that occurs at each stage for both organisms

nodes.label: Metamorphic and non-metamorphic cycles differ in structure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between metamorphic life cycles (dramatic change in body form between stages) and non-metamorphic cycles (gradual growth without structural transformation), and give examples of each.
criteria: Distinguishes metamorphic from non-metamorphic life cycles with at least one example of each
Explains what 'metamorphosis' means in terms of change in body form between life stages

descriptors.title: Soils, rocks and minerals
descriptors.description: compare the observable properties of soils, rocks and minerals and investigate why they are important Earth resources

nodes.label: Soils have observable properties and components
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the observable components of soil samples (pebbles, sand, clay, plant matter, living things) and compare the properties of different soils using observable evidence.
criteria: Identifies at least three components in a soil sample using observation
Compares two soil samples using at least two property terms with observable evidence

nodes.label: Rocks and minerals have observable properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe and compare observable properties of rocks and minerals (colour, texture, grain size, crystal size, hardness, lustre), and explain that minerals are the building blocks of rocks.
criteria: Describes at least two observable properties for each of three rock or mineral samples
Explains that minerals are the building blocks of rocks

nodes.label: Soils, rocks and minerals are important Earth resources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why soils, rocks and minerals are important resources for living things — including how living things depend on soils and how humans use rocks and minerals — and give specific examples of each.
criteria: Gives at least two examples of how living things depend on soil with explanation
Gives at least two examples of human use of rocks or minerals, connecting the use to a property of the material

descriptors.title: Heat energy and transfer
descriptors.description: identify sources of heat energy and examine how temperature changes when heat energy is transferred from one object to another

nodes.label: Heat energy comes from identifiable sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and classify sources of heat energy in everyday and natural contexts (sun, fire, electrical devices, geothermal, friction, body heat) and explain that heat is a form of energy.
criteria: Identifies at least four sources of heat energy across at least two categories
Explains that heat is a form of energy that can be transferred and measured

nodes.label: Heat transfers from warmer to cooler objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that heat energy transfers from a warmer object to a cooler object when they are in contact, describe what happens to the temperature of each object during the transfer, and use temperature measurements to support their explanation.
criteria: Explains that heat transfers from warmer to cooler objects, not from cold to warm
Describes what happens to the temperature of both objects during heat transfer (warm cools, cool warms) until they reach the same temperature
Uses thermometer observations to support the explanation

nodes.label: Materials differ in how well they conduct or insulate heat
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that some materials (conductors) transfer heat quickly and others (insulators) transfer heat slowly, give examples of each, and connect material selection to everyday uses for keeping things hot or cold.
criteria: Identifies at least two conductors and two insulators with examples
Explains the difference between a conductor and an insulator in terms of how quickly heat transfers
Gives at least one everyday example where conductor or insulator properties determine material selection

descriptors.title: Science collaboration and building on others' work
descriptors.description: examine why advances in science are often the result of collaboration or build on the work of others

nodes.label: Scientific advances build on prior work
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe at least one example where a scientific advance built on the prior work of others, explaining what earlier knowledge was required and how the new discovery extended or depended on it.
criteria: Describes one example of a scientific advance that built on prior work
Identifies the earlier knowledge that was required and explains how the new contribution depended on it

nodes.label: Collaboration across disciplines and institutions advances science
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why complex scientific questions often require collaboration across disciplines, institutions or countries, and describe at least one example where such collaboration produced an advance.
criteria: Describes one example of collaboration across at least two disciplines or groups
Explains what each contributor brought to the collaboration and why a single discipline could not have answered the question alone

descriptors.title: Scientific knowledge used by communities
descriptors.description: investigate how scientific knowledge is used by individuals and communities to identify problems, consider responses and make decisions

nodes.label: Scientific knowledge helps identify and define problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how scientific knowledge enables people to identify and precisely define a problem — distinguishing between a symptom (what is observed) and a cause (what the knowledge explains).
criteria: Describes one example where scientific knowledge enabled a problem to be identified
Explains what the knowledge was and how it transformed an observation into a defined problem with a cause

nodes.label: Scientific knowledge informs decisions and responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine how communities use scientific knowledge to evaluate options and make decisions — explaining what knowledge was used, what options were considered, and why a particular response was chosen.
criteria: Describes one example where a community used scientific knowledge to make a decision
Explains what knowledge was used, what options were considered, and why the chosen response was selected

descriptors.title: Questioning and predicting
descriptors.description: pose investigable questions to identify patterns and test relationships and make reasoned predictions

nodes.label: Investigable questions test relationships between variables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can pose investigable questions that specifically target a relationship between two variables — framed as 'Does X affect Y?' or 'How does X change when Y changes?' — and explain what makes a question investigable.
criteria: Poses a question that targets a relationship between two named variables
Explains why the question is investigable — what would be changed and what would be measured

nodes.label: Reasoned predictions are justified with prior scientific knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make reasoned predictions that are explicitly justified using prior scientific knowledge — distinguishing a reasoned prediction from an observation-based prediction by the nature of the justification.
criteria: Makes a prediction and explicitly states the prior scientific knowledge (not just prior observation) that justifies it
Identifies what outcome would confirm or challenge the prediction

descriptors.title: Planning and conducting
descriptors.description: plan and conduct repeatable investigations to answer questions, including, as appropriate, deciding the variables to be changed, measured and controlled in fair tests; describing potential risks; planning for the safe use of equipment and materials; and identifying required permissions to conduct investigations on Country/Place

nodes.label: Repeatable investigations require a recorded, reproducible method
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan and record an investigation method in sufficient detail that another person could repeat it, and explain why repeatability is important for reliable findings.
criteria: Records an investigation method in sufficient detail for another student to repeat it
Explains why repeatability is important for the reliability of findings

nodes.label: Variables, risks and permissions are identified in planning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can independently decide which variables to change, measure and control in a fair test, describe potential risks, plan safe equipment use, and identify any permissions required for field investigations.
criteria: Independently identifies variables to change, measure and control without a provided scaffold
Describes at least one potential risk and the planned safety measure to address it

descriptors.title: Processing and representing data
descriptors.description: construct and use appropriate representations, including tables, graphs and visual or physical models, to organise and process data and information and describe patterns, trends and relationships

nodes.label: Representations are selected and constructed for a given data type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select an appropriate representation type for a given data set or relationship and construct it accurately — with correct labels, conventions and structure.
criteria: Selects a representation type appropriate to the data or relationship and explains why it suits the purpose
Constructs the representation with correct labels, units and conventions for the chosen type

nodes.label: Representations are used to identify and describe patterns, trends and relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a completed representation to identify a pattern, trend or relationship in the data and describe what it means in the context of the investigation question.
criteria: Identifies at least one pattern, trend or relationship in a completed representation
Describes what the pattern or relationship means in the context of the investigation question — not just what the graph shows, but what it tells us

descriptors.title: Evaluating
descriptors.description: compare methods and findings with those of others, recognise possible sources of error, pose questions for further investigation and select evidence to draw reasoned conclusions

nodes.label: Errors are identified and their effect on findings is explained
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific sources of error in an investigation method (uncontrolled variables, measurement errors, environmental changes) and explain how each error could affect the findings and conclusions.
criteria: Identifies at least two specific sources of error in an investigation method
Explains how each identified error could affect the findings or conclusion

nodes.label: Evidence is selected to draw reasoned conclusions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select relevant evidence from a data set, use it to draw a reasoned conclusion, and explain why the selected evidence supports the conclusion while other data does not.
criteria: Distinguishes between data and evidence for a given investigation
Selects at least two pieces of evidence that support a named conclusion and explains why each is relevant
Draws a reasoned conclusion that does not overclaim beyond the selected evidence

descriptors.title: Communicating
descriptors.description: write and create texts to communicate ideas and findings for specific purposes and audiences, including selection of language features, using digital tools as appropriate

nodes.label: Language features are selected deliberately to shape meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how vocabulary and sentence structure contribute to the meaning and effectiveness of a science text, and make deliberate language choices in their own writing to serve their communication purpose.
criteria: Identifies at least two language features in a science text and explains how each contributes to meaning
Makes at least two deliberate language choices in their own writing and explains the reasoning

nodes.label: Science texts serve specific purposes with appropriate conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write and create science texts in at least two different forms (scientific report, persuasive text, digital presentation) with appropriate conventions for each form, tailored to a specific purpose and audience.
criteria: Produces a science text in a given form using appropriate conventions
Selects vocabulary appropriate to the purpose and audience
Justifies at least one language choice in terms of how it serves the communication purpose

descriptors.title: Structural features and survival
descriptors.description: examine how particular structural features and behaviours of living things enable their survival in specific habitats

nodes.label: Structural features are physical characteristics that aid survival
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify structural features of plants and animals and explain how each feature addresses a specific survival challenge in the organism's habitat.
criteria: Identifies at least three structural features of a named organism
Explains how each feature addresses a specific survival challenge in the organism's habitat

nodes.label: Behaviours also enable survival in specific habitats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify behavioural adaptations of organisms and explain how each behaviour addresses a specific survival challenge — distinguishing behavioural from structural adaptations.
criteria: Identifies at least two behavioural adaptations of a named organism and explains the survival function of each
Distinguishes between a structural feature and a behavioural adaptation for the same organism

nodes.label: Features and behaviours match the challenges of specific habitats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can connect the structural features and behaviours of an organism to the specific physical conditions and challenges of its habitat — explaining why this organism is well-suited to this habitat and less suited to a different one.
criteria: Connects at least two features or behaviours to specific physical conditions of a named habitat
Predicts at least one challenge an organism would face if placed in a different habitat, with reasoning

descriptors.title: Weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition
descriptors.description: describe how weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition cause slow or rapid change to Earth's surface

nodes.label: Weathering breaks down rocks in place
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish weathering from erosion — explaining that weathering breaks down rock material in place through mechanical and biological means — and identify agents of weathering with examples.
criteria: Explains that weathering breaks down rock material in place without moving it
Names at least two weathering agents and explains the mechanism by which each breaks down rock

nodes.label: Erosion, transportation and deposition move and redistribute material
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that erosion picks up and moves weathered material, transportation carries it, and deposition lays it down in a new location — describing the agents involved (water, wind, ice, gravity) and the landforms each process produces.
criteria: Explains the three-stage sequence: erosion (picks up) → transportation (carries) → deposition (lays down)
Names at least two agents of erosion and identifies a landform feature produced by each

nodes.label: Human activity changes erosion rates
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how human activity alters natural erosion rates and predict the consequences of specific land use changes on local landscapes.
criteria: Explains at least one mechanism by which human activity increases erosion rates
Describes at least one strategy that mitigates erosion and explains how it reduces the rate

descriptors.title: Light
descriptors.description: identify sources of light, recognise that light travels in a straight path and describe how shadows are formed and light can be reflected and refracted

nodes.label: Light travels in straight paths from sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify natural and artificial light sources, explain that light travels in straight paths (rays) from a source, and use this to explain why objects cast shadows.
criteria: Names at least two natural and two artificial light sources
Explains that light travels in straight paths (rays) from a source
Uses straight-line travel to explain why an object casts a shadow

nodes.label: Shadows form when light is blocked
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how shadows form when an opaque object blocks light, describe how shadow size and shape change with the position and distance of the light source, and represent shadow formation using ray diagrams.
criteria: Explains shadow formation using the straight-line travel of light being blocked by an object
Predicts how shadow size will change when the light source or object position changes, with reasoning
Draws a ray diagram showing shadow formation

nodes.label: Light reflects off surfaces and refracts when changing medium
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain reflection as light bouncing off a surface in a predictable direction, describe refraction as the bending of light when it passes between different media, give everyday examples of each, and draw ray diagrams for reflection.
criteria: Explains reflection using a ray diagram showing light bouncing off a surface
Explains refraction as the bending of light when it passes between different media, with an everyday example
Distinguishes reflection from refraction as different interactions of light with matter

descriptors.title: Particle model of matter
descriptors.description: explain observable properties of solids, liquids and gases by modelling the motion and arrangement of particles

nodes.label: Gases have observable properties distinct from solids and liquids
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe observable properties of gases — including that gases have mass, can be compressed, and take the shape and volume of their container — and distinguish these from the properties of solids and liquids.
criteria: States at least two observable properties of gases that distinguish them from solids and liquids
Provides evidence that gases have mass

nodes.label: Particle arrangement and motion explain state properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a particle model to explain the observable properties of each state — describing how particle arrangement (close/far apart) and motion (vibrating/flowing/moving freely) differ across solids, liquids and gases.
criteria: Describes particle arrangement and motion for each of the three states
Uses the particle model to explain at least two observable properties — one for solids and one for gases

nodes.label: State changes are explained by changes in particle behaviour
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain state changes (melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation) using the particle model — describing how adding or removing heat energy changes particle motion and the transitions between states.
criteria: Explains at least one state change using particle arrangement and motion — describing what happens to particles when heat is added or removed
Explains why mass is conserved during a state change using the particle model

descriptors.title: Physical conditions and survival
descriptors.description: investigate the physical conditions of a habitat and analyse how the growth and survival of living things is affected by changing physical conditions

nodes.label: Habitats have measurable physical conditions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the physical conditions of an aquatic or terrestrial habitat — including temperature, light availability, salinity, soil type, moisture and pH — and explain how these conditions vary over time.
criteria: Identifies at least three physical conditions of a named habitat
Explains how at least one physical condition varies over time in the habitat

nodes.label: Changing physical conditions affect growth and survival
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how changes in physical conditions affect the growth and survival of living things — using investigation data or case study evidence to support their analysis.
criteria: Describes how a change in a named physical condition affects the growth or survival of a named organism
Uses evidence (investigation data or case study) to support the analysis

nodes.label: Human activity changes physical conditions and affects living things
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how human-caused changes to physical conditions affect living things, examine community and scientific responses, and predict the impact of specific condition changes on named organisms.
criteria: Describes a human-caused change to a physical condition and its effect on a named organism, with the mechanism explained
Describes at least one scientific or community response to a human-caused condition change

descriptors.title: Earth, sun and solar system
descriptors.description: describe the movement of Earth and other planets relative to the sun and model how Earth's tilt, rotation on its axis and revolution around the sun relate to cyclic observable phenomena, including variable day and night length

nodes.label: Earth and planets orbit the sun; gravity keeps them in orbit
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the relative positions and movements of the sun and planets in the solar system, explain that gravity keeps planets in orbit, and appreciate the scale of distances involved.
criteria: Describes the movement of Earth and at least two other planets relative to the sun
Explains that gravity keeps planets in orbit around the sun

nodes.label: Earth's rotation causes day and night
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a model to explain how Earth's rotation on its axis causes day and night, and explain why different places on Earth experience daylight at different times.
criteria: Explains that day and night are caused by Earth's rotation on its axis
Uses a model or diagram to show that the side of Earth facing the sun has day and the side facing away has night

nodes.label: Earth's tilt and revolution cause variable day length and seasons
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how Earth's axial tilt, combined with its revolution around the sun, causes different hemispheres to receive different amounts of sunlight at different times of year — producing variable day length and seasons.
criteria: Explains that Earth's axial tilt causes one hemisphere to receive more sunlight than the other at different times of year
Uses a model or diagram to show why the Southern and Northern hemispheres have opposite seasons
Explains why day length varies between summer and winter at the same location

descriptors.title: Electrical circuits
descriptors.description: investigate the transfer and transformation of energy in electrical circuits, including the role of circuit components, insulators and conductors

nodes.label: A circuit requires a complete conducting path and energy source
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what is required for an electrical circuit to work — a complete conducting path from and back to the energy source — and identify what happens to the circuit when the path is broken.
criteria: Explains that a circuit requires a complete conducting path and an energy source
Explains what happens to the circuit when the path is broken and why

nodes.label: Conductors allow electricity to flow; insulators do not
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish electrical conductors from insulators, classify common materials, explain why conductors and insulators are used in specific components, and connect this to safe electrical design.
criteria: Classifies at least four materials as electrical conductors or insulators
Explains why a wire has a metal core with a plastic coating — connecting conductor and insulator properties to a real design decision

nodes.label: Electrical energy is transferred and transformed by circuit components
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how electrical energy is transferred through a circuit and transformed by components into light, heat and sound, and represent circuits using standard conventions.
criteria: Explains how at least two different circuit components transform electrical energy into other forms
Draws a circuit diagram using standard symbols
Connects electrical energy transformation in a circuit to the general concept that energy changes form

descriptors.title: Reversible and irreversible changes
descriptors.description: compare reversible changes, including dissolving and changes of state, and irreversible changes, including cooking and rusting that produce new substances

nodes.label: Reversible changes do not produce new substances
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that reversible changes — including dissolving and state changes — do not produce new substances, describe how dissolved substances can be recovered, and give examples of reversible changes used in recycling.
criteria: Explains that dissolving is reversible — the dissolved substance can be recovered
Describes at least one method for recovering a dissolved substance
Explains that reversible changes do not produce new substances

nodes.label: Irreversible changes produce new substances
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that irreversible changes produce new substances with different properties, identify observable evidence of new substance formation, and give examples of common irreversible changes.
criteria: Explains that irreversible changes produce new substances with different properties
Names at least two observable indicators that an irreversible change has occurred
Distinguishes an irreversible change from a reversible change by the presence or absence of new substance formation

nodes.label: Reversible and irreversible changes are compared systematically
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare reversible and irreversible changes systematically — using the criterion of new substance formation — classify a range of everyday changes correctly, and explain how this distinction is used in practical contexts.
criteria: Classifies at least four everyday changes as reversible or irreversible using the new-substance criterion
Correctly classifies at least one ambiguous case (e.g. dissolving) with reasoning
Explains how the reversible/irreversible distinction is applied in a practical context

descriptors.title: Evidence changes knowledge
descriptors.description: explain how new evidence or different perspectives can lead to changes in scientific knowledge

nodes.label: Scientific knowledge is based on evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that scientific knowledge is built from evidence and that the type and quality of evidence matters
criteria: States that scientific knowledge is based on evidence
Gives one correct example of evidence supporting a scientific idea
Does not confuse evidence with opinion or belief

nodes.label: New evidence changes scientific understanding
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how new evidence — from new technology, methods or discoveries — has led to changes in scientific understanding
criteria: Names a specific example where scientific understanding changed due to new evidence
Explains what the new evidence was and how it caused the change
Does not describe the change as science being 'wrong before'

nodes.label: Different perspectives shape knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how different perspectives — including cultural, historical and disciplinary — contribute to the development of scientific knowledge
criteria: Names a specific example where a different perspective contributed to scientific knowledge
Explains the contribution rather than just naming the perspective
Recognises that multiple perspectives can coexist and contribute to understanding

nodes.label: Evidence and perspectives together refine knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the interplay of new evidence and different perspectives leads to ongoing refinement of scientific knowledge
criteria: Explains how both new evidence and different perspectives contributed to a knowledge change
Identifies that scientific knowledge refinement is an ongoing process

descriptors.title: Culture shapes scientific knowledge
descriptors.description: investigate how cultural perspectives and world views influence the development of scientific knowledge

nodes.label: Scientists bring perspectives to their work
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that scientists' personal beliefs, cultural backgrounds and societal contexts influence the questions they pursue
criteria: Names a specific example where perspective influenced a scientific question or approach
Explains the connection between the perspective and the scientific work
Does not treat perspective as automatically introducing bias or error

nodes.label: Cultural knowledge systems contribute to science
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how knowledge systems from different cultures contribute to scientific understanding
criteria: Names a specific cultural knowledge contribution to scientific understanding
Explains what the contribution is rather than just naming the culture
Does not frame cultural knowledge as inferior to or separate from science

nodes.label: Different perspectives on science-society issues
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why different people hold different perspectives on science-related issues and why recognising this matters
criteria: Identifies a science-society issue with multiple perspectives
Explains why different groups hold different views
Recognises that considering multiple perspectives improves decision-making

nodes.label: Culture shapes the development of scientific knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how cultural perspectives and world views have influenced the development of scientific knowledge across multiple examples
criteria: Explains how a cultural perspective influenced the development of specific scientific knowledge
Connects the perspective to the knowledge outcome rather than just describing each separately

descriptors.title: Science responses impact society
descriptors.description: examine how proposed scientific responses to contemporary issues may impact on society and explore ethical, environmental, social and economic considerations

nodes.label: Scientific responses to contemporary issues
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify proposed scientific responses to contemporary issues and describe the intended impact
criteria: Identifies a proposed scientific response and the contemporary issue it addresses
Describes the intended impact of the response
Distinguishes the scientific response from a political or social response

nodes.label: Impacts can be positive and negative
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine both intended and unintended impacts of a scientific response on society and the environment
criteria: Identifies both an intended and an unintended impact of a scientific response
Explains why the unintended impact occurs
Does not frame the response as simply good or bad

nodes.label: Ethical, environmental, social and economic considerations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore ethical, environmental, social and economic considerations associated with a proposed scientific response
criteria: Identifies at least two types of consideration relevant to a specific response
Explains why each consideration matters for that response
Distinguishes between the consideration types rather than conflating them

nodes.label: Evaluating scientific responses with multiple considerations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine a proposed scientific response by weighing multiple considerations and explaining why stakeholders may reach different conclusions
criteria: Examines a scientific response using at least two consideration types
Explains why different stakeholders evaluate the response differently
Connects stakeholder conclusions to their priorities rather than framing disagreement as ignorance

descriptors.title: Science communication shapes policy
descriptors.description: explore the role of science communication in informing individual viewpoints and community policies and regulations

nodes.label: Science communication takes many forms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify different forms of science communication and recognise that how science is communicated affects what people understand
criteria: Identifies at least two forms of science communication
Explains how each form reaches a different audience
Recognises that communication choices affect what people understand

nodes.label: Communication informs individual viewpoints
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how science communication informs and changes individual viewpoints on science-related issues
criteria: Names a specific example where science communication changed viewpoints
Explains what was communicated and how viewpoints changed
Distinguishes the role of communication from the knowledge itself

nodes.label: Communication shapes community policies and regulations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how science communication leads to changes in community policies and regulations
criteria: Names a specific example where science communication led to a policy or regulation change
Explains the pathway from communication to policy outcome
Distinguishes the policy change from the underlying scientific knowledge

nodes.label: The role of science communication in society
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how science communication plays an ongoing role in informing viewpoints and shaping policies across different contexts
criteria: Explains how communication choices connected to both viewpoint and policy outcomes
Identifies what made the communication effective or ineffective

descriptors.title: Explore models and test relationships
descriptors.description: develop investigable questions, reasoned predictions and hypotheses to explore scientific models, identify patterns and test relationships

nodes.label: Investigable vs non-investigable questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish investigable from non-investigable questions and explain what makes a question investigable
criteria: Correctly classifies at least 3 questions as investigable or non-investigable
States at least two features that make a question investigable
Does not confuse 'interesting' with 'investigable'

nodes.label: Developing investigable questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop investigable questions to explore scientific models or test relationships between variables
criteria: Develops an investigable question that identifies variables or a model to explore
The question is testable with available methods and resources
Explains how the question connects to the model or relationship being investigated

nodes.label: Predictions and hypotheses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can formulate reasoned predictions and hypotheses that include a variable, predicted outcome and reasoning
criteria: Develops a hypothesis that includes a variable, predicted outcome and reasoning
Distinguishes a prediction from a hypothesis
The reasoning in the hypothesis is scientifically plausible

descriptors.title: Plan reproducible investigations
descriptors.description: plan and conduct reproducible investigations to answer questions and test hypotheses, including identifying variables and assumptions and, as appropriate, recognising and managing risks, considering ethical issues and recognising key considerations regarding heritage sites and artefacts on Country/Place

nodes.label: Variables and assumptions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify independent, dependent and controlled variables and recognise assumptions about controlled variables
criteria: Correctly identifies independent, dependent and controlled variables in a given method
Names at least one assumption about a controlled variable
Explains why controlling variables matters for the investigation

nodes.label: Planning reproducible methods
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a method that another person could reproduce to obtain comparable results
criteria: Plans a method with sufficient detail for another person to reproduce
Method logically tests the stated hypothesis
Peer review confirms the method is followable

nodes.label: Risks, ethics and heritage considerations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and manage risks, consider ethical issues and recognise heritage site protocols when planning investigations
criteria: Identifies at least one risk and suggests how to manage it
Identifies at least one ethical consideration relevant to the investigation
Recognises that heritage sites and artefacts require specific protocols

descriptors.title: Select equipment and record data
descriptors.description: select and use equipment to generate and record data with precision, using digital tools as appropriate

nodes.label: Selecting appropriate equipment
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select equipment appropriate to an investigation's measurement needs and justify the choice
criteria: Selects equipment appropriate to the measurement task
Justifies the choice based on measurement range or precision
Does not select equipment that cannot measure the expected values

nodes.label: Recording data with precision
nodes.checkpoint: Students can record data in organised formats using correct units and appropriate precision
criteria: Records data using correct standard units
Precision is appropriate to the equipment used
Data table is organised with clear headings and units

nodes.label: Using digital tools for data generation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use digital tools to generate more precise or efficient data and explain the advantage over manual methods
criteria: Identifies a digital tool appropriate for a given investigation
Explains the advantage of the digital tool over a manual alternative
Uses the tool to generate data with appropriate precision

descriptors.title: Select tables, graphs and models
descriptors.description: select and construct appropriate representations, including tables, graphs, models and mathematical relationships, to organise and process data and information

nodes.label: Choosing appropriate representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select an appropriate representation type for a given data set based on data characteristics
criteria: Selects a representation type appropriate for the data characteristics
Explains why the chosen representation suits the data
Does not default to one representation type regardless of data

nodes.label: Constructing representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct tables, graphs, food webs, dichotomous keys and other models to organise data and information
criteria: Constructs a representation with correct labels, scales and conventions
Representation accurately reflects the source data
Uses the representation to describe at least one pattern

nodes.label: Processing data through representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use representations including mathematical relationships to process and analyse data
criteria: Uses a representation to identify and describe a pattern
Description is supported by specific reference to the data
Does not over-interpret the data beyond what the representation shows

descriptors.title: Identify patterns and anomalies
descriptors.description: analyse data and information to describe patterns, trends and relationships and identify anomalies

nodes.label: Describing patterns and trends
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe patterns and trends in data sets
criteria: Identifies a pattern or trend in a data set
Describes the pattern using appropriate language
Does not confuse correlation with a single data point

nodes.label: Identifying relationships in data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse data to identify and describe relationships between variables
criteria: Identifies a relationship between two variables
Describes the relationship type (positive, negative or non-linear)
Connects the relationship to the variables involved, not just the trend direction

nodes.label: Identifying and explaining anomalies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify anomalies in data and investigate their effect on observed patterns or relationships
criteria: Identifies an anomaly in a data set
Explains why the anomaly does not fit the observed pattern
Does not automatically discard anomalies without considering whether they are meaningful

descriptors.title: Analyse methods and claims
descriptors.description: analyse methods, conclusions and claims for assumptions, possible sources of error, conflicting evidence and unanswered questions

nodes.label: Identifying sources of error
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify possible sources of error in an investigation method and suggest improvements
criteria: Identifies a specific source of error (not just 'human error')
Explains how the error affects the data or results
Suggests a specific improvement to reduce the error

nodes.label: Evaluating methods and assumptions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate an investigation method by identifying assumptions about controlled variables and assessing whether the method tests the hypothesis
criteria: Identifies at least one assumption about a controlled variable
Explains why the assumption matters for the investigation's validity
Assesses whether the method tests the stated hypothesis

nodes.label: Evaluating conclusions and claims
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse conclusions and claims for conflicting evidence and unanswered questions
criteria: Identifies evidence that both supports and conflicts with a claim
Identifies at least one unanswered question arising from the evidence
Does not treat a conclusion as proven simply because some evidence supports it

descriptors.title: Construct evidence-based arguments
descriptors.description: construct evidence-based arguments to support conclusions or evaluate claims and consider any ethical issues and cultural protocols associated with using or citing secondary data or information

nodes.label: Drawing conclusions from evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw a conclusion from evidence that supports or rejects a hypothesis and identify the evidence used
criteria: Draws a conclusion that is consistent with the evidence
Identifies the specific evidence that supports the conclusion
States whether the evidence supports or rejects the hypothesis

nodes.label: Constructing evidence-based arguments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct an argument supported by evidence and reasoning to support a conclusion or evaluate a claim
criteria: Constructs an argument that links evidence to a conclusion through reasoning
The reasoning explains why the evidence supports the conclusion
Does not simply list evidence without connecting it to the conclusion

nodes.label: Ethics of using secondary data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can consider ethical issues and cultural protocols associated with using or citing secondary data or information
criteria: Identifies an ethical issue or cultural protocol relevant to using secondary data
Explains why the issue matters for the integrity of the argument
Recognises that cultural knowledge requires specific protocols for use and citation

descriptors.title: Communicate ideas and arguments
descriptors.description: write and create texts to communicate ideas, findings and arguments for specific purposes and audiences, including selection of appropriate language and text features, using digital tools as appropriate

nodes.label: Purpose, audience and text type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the purpose and audience of scientific texts and select an appropriate text type
criteria: Identifies the purpose and target audience of a scientific text
Explains how the text type suits the audience
Does not assume all scientific communication uses the same format

nodes.label: Language and text features for science communication
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and use appropriate language and text features including diagrams, graphical representations and data
criteria: Includes at least one diagram or graphical representation
Representation is referenced in the text, not just appended
Language is appropriate for the stated audience

nodes.label: Communicating for specific purposes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write and create texts that communicate ideas, findings and arguments effectively for a specific purpose and audience
criteria: Produces a communication for a specific purpose and audience
Text type and language features are appropriate to the purpose
Communication includes ideas, findings or arguments — not just description

descriptors.title: Classification and biodiversity
descriptors.description: investigate the role of classification in ordering and organising the diversity of life on Earth and use and develop classification tools including dichotomous keys

nodes.label: Purpose of classification
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why classification is useful for organising and communicating about living things
criteria: Names at least two reasons why classification is useful (e.g. identification, communication)
Gives a correct everyday example of classification
Does not confuse classification with simple sorting or listing

nodes.label: Taxonomy: major groups and kingdoms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can place organisms into major taxonomic groups using observable features and justify their classification
criteria: Correctly places 5 familiar organisms into kingdoms with observable feature justification
Identifies at least one organism that is difficult to classify and explains why

nodes.label: Using dichotomous keys
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a dichotomous key to identify organisms by applying binary decisions based on observable features
criteria: Follows all decision points in a provided key to reach correct identifications
Names the observable feature used at each decision point
Explains why an incorrect path leads to a wrong outcome

nodes.label: Constructing dichotomous keys
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a dichotomous key that correctly classifies a set of organisms using observable features
criteria: Constructs a key that correctly classifies all organisms in a given set
Key uses binary observable features at each decision point
Peer testing confirms key produces correct identifications

nodes.label: Classification systems change over time
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how classification systems change in response to new evidence and evaluate what this reveals about scientific knowledge
criteria: Names a real reclassification event and the evidence that caused it
Explains whether reclassification weakens or strengthens confidence in science

descriptors.title: Food webs and ecosystems
descriptors.description: use models, including food webs, to represent matter and energy flow in ecosystems and predict the impact of changing abiotic and biotic factors on populations

nodes.label: From food chains to food webs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a food web and identify the roles of producers, consumers and decomposers including microorganisms
criteria: Correctly places all organisms in a food web into producer, consumer or decomposer roles
Arrows show direction of energy flow, not just feeding relationships
Includes microorganisms in the decomposer role

nodes.label: Matter and energy flow
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the direction and loss of energy through trophic levels and distinguish energy flow from matter cycling
criteria: States that energy is lost at each trophic level
Correctly distinguishes energy flow from matter cycling in an explanation
Traces the direction of energy through at least 3 trophic levels

nodes.label: Abiotic factors and population effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can predict and explain how a change to an abiotic factor cascades through populations in a food web
criteria: Correctly defines abiotic factor and gives 3 examples
Predicts the effect of one abiotic change on one population with reasoning
Identifies at least one other population affected by the cascade

nodes.label: Biotic factors and population effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can predict and explain how a change to a biotic factor cascades through populations in a food web
criteria: Correctly defines biotic factor and gives 3 examples
Predicts the effect of removing one species with food web reasoning
Traces at least one cascade effect beyond the immediate population

nodes.label: Models, limitations and predictions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the limitations of food web models and explain how these affect the reliability of predictions
criteria: Identifies at least one limitation of food web models
Explains how that limitation affects the reliability of a specific prediction

descriptors.title: Earth-Sun-Moon system
descriptors.description: model cyclic changes in the relative positions of the Earth, sun and moon and explain how these cycles cause eclipses and influence predictable phenomena on Earth, including seasons and tides

nodes.label: Earth's rotation, revolution and axial tilt
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish Earth's rotation from revolution and explain how axial tilt relates to observable changes across a year
criteria: Correctly distinguishes rotation from revolution
Links rotation to day/night and revolution to the year
Identifies that Earth's axis is tilted

nodes.label: Moon phases and the lunar cycle
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain moon phases as a result of the moon's position relative to Earth and sun and sequence them correctly
criteria: Correctly sequences all 8 moon phases
Explains phases as caused by the moon's position, not Earth's shadow
Does not confuse moon phases with eclipses

nodes.label: Eclipses: solar and lunar
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the conditions required for solar and lunar eclipses and why eclipses do not occur every month
criteria: States the conditions required for both solar and lunar eclipses
Correctly distinguishes umbra from penumbra
Explains why eclipses don't occur every month

nodes.label: Seasons
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain seasons as caused by axial tilt and correctly relate tilt to solar angle and day length at different latitudes
criteria: Explains seasons as caused by axial tilt, not distance from the sun
Links tilt to solar angle and day length
Correctly identifies opposite seasons in Northern and Southern hemispheres

nodes.label: Tides
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain tides as caused by the moon's gravitational pull and distinguish spring from neap tides by moon position
criteria: Explains tides as caused by the moon's gravitational pull
Correctly identifies spring and neap tides
Links spring and neap tides to moon positions

descriptors.title: Forces and motion
descriptors.description: investigate and represent balanced and unbalanced forces, including gravitational force, acting on objects, and relate changes in an object's motion to its mass and the magnitude and direction of forces acting on it

nodes.label: Forces as vectors: magnitude and direction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent forces on an object as vectors showing correct magnitude and direction and name the forces
criteria: Represents at least 2 forces on an object with correct arrow direction and relative size
Names each force represented
Diagram is consistent with the described scenario

nodes.label: Balanced forces and equilibrium
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify whether forces on an object are balanced or unbalanced and predict the resulting motion state
criteria: Correctly identifies balanced vs unbalanced forces in a given diagram
States that balanced forces mean no change in motion — not that no forces are acting
Predicts the motion state from a force diagram

nodes.label: Unbalanced forces and changes in motion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that unbalanced forces cause a change in motion and represent this with force diagrams
criteria: States that unbalanced forces cause a change in motion
Gives 2 examples with correct force diagrams
Identifies both speed and direction as possible changes

nodes.label: Gravitational force and mass
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish mass from weight, explain gravitational force as dependent on mass, and calculate weight from mass
criteria: Correctly distinguishes mass from weight with definitions
Calculates weight correctly given mass and g
Explains gravitational force as dependent on mass — not just Earth's pull

nodes.label: Relating force, mass and motion change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the qualitative relationship between force, mass and acceleration and interpret data from force investigations
criteria: States the qualitative relationship between force, mass and acceleration
Correctly predicts which object accelerates more under the same force
Identifies the pattern in data from a force investigation

descriptors.title: Particle theory and properties
descriptors.description: use particle theory to describe the arrangement of particles in a substance, including the motion of and attraction between particles, and relate this to the properties of the substance

nodes.label: Introducing the particle model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can match particle diagrams to states of matter and state the key ideas of particle theory
criteria: Matches particle diagrams to correct states of matter
States the 4 key ideas of particle theory
Identifies differences in arrangement, motion and attraction across states

nodes.label: Particle arrangement, motion and attraction in each state
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe particle arrangement, motion and attraction for each state and explain observable properties using this model
criteria: Describes particle arrangement, motion and attraction for each state
Explains why solids hold shape and gases fill containers using particle theory
Does not treat particle diagrams as decorative — uses them to support reasoning

nodes.label: Explaining physical properties using particle theory
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use particle theory to explain physical properties of substances including compressibility, viscosity and density
criteria: Uses particle theory to explain at least 2 physical properties of a given substance
Explanation references arrangement, motion or attraction — not just state labels
Correctly links a named property to the relevant particle behaviour

nodes.label: Changes of state and energy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain changes of state using particle theory and correctly identify energy input or output for each change
criteria: Explains melting, freezing, evaporation and condensation using particle theory
Correctly identifies energy input or output for each change
Does not confuse temperature change with state change during plateau regions

nodes.label: Particle theory as a model: scope and limits
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the scope and limitations of the particle model and explain what evidence supports it
criteria: Identifies one phenomenon particle theory explains well and one it does not
Gives a reason for each based on the model's assumptions

descriptors.title: Pure substances and mixtures
descriptors.description: use a particle model to describe differences between pure substances and mixtures and apply understanding of properties of substances to separate mixtures

nodes.label: Pure substances vs mixtures at the particle level
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish pure substances from mixtures using particle diagrams and classify familiar materials correctly
criteria: Correctly distinguishes pure substance from mixture using particle diagrams
Classifies 5 familiar materials correctly with justification
Does not confuse homogeneous mixtures (e.g. solutions) with pure substances

nodes.label: Properties as the basis for separation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that separation techniques exploit differences in physical properties and match property differences to techniques
criteria: States that separation exploits differences in physical properties
Correctly matches at least 3 property differences to separation techniques
Explains why a chosen technique would work for a given mixture

nodes.label: Filtration and evaporation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform or describe filtration and evaporation and justify their use for appropriate mixtures
criteria: Correctly describes or performs filtration and evaporation
Identifies a mixture appropriate for each technique with property reasoning
Explains why the chosen technique works using property differences

nodes.label: Distillation and chromatography
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the principles of distillation and chromatography and identify mixtures each technique is appropriate for
criteria: Describes the principle of distillation and chromatography
Identifies a mixture appropriate for each technique
Distinguishes when distillation is preferred over evaporation

nodes.label: Selecting and justifying separation techniques
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and justify an appropriate separation technique for an unfamiliar mixture using property differences
criteria: Selects an appropriate technique for an unfamiliar mixture
Justifies the choice using property differences
Identifies at least one technique that would not work and explains why

descriptors.title: Cells as basic units
descriptors.description: recognise cells as the basic units of living things, compare plant and animal cells, and describe the functions of specialised cell structures and organelles

nodes.label: Cellular scale — why cells are invisible and require magnification
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the scale of cells relative to organisms and explain why microscopes are required to observe them.
criteria: States that cells are microscopic and not visible to the naked eye
Explains that microscopes were necessary to discover and observe cells
Gives an approximate size comparison between a cell and a familiar object

nodes.label: Cell theory — all living things are made of cells
nodes.checkpoint: Students can state that all living things — including plants, fungi and single-celled organisms — are made of cells, and distinguish single-celled from multicellular organisms.
criteria: States that all living things are made of cells
Includes plants and single-celled organisms explicitly in this claim
Distinguishes single-celled from multicellular organisms with examples from each

nodes.label: Cell structures shared by plant and animal cells — nucleus, membrane, cytoplasm
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the function of structures present in both plant and animal cells: nucleus, cell membrane and cytoplasm.
criteria: States the function of nucleus, cell membrane and cytoplasm
Explains at least one structural feature of each that relates to its function
Identifies these three as structures present in both plant and animal cells

nodes.label: Plant-specific structures — cell wall, chloroplasts, large central vacuole
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify cell wall, chloroplasts and large central vacuole as plant-specific structures and explain the functional significance of each.
criteria: Identifies cell wall, chloroplasts and large central vacuole as plant-specific structures
Explains the function of each plant-specific structure
Connects each plant-specific structure to an organism-level need that animal cells do not have

nodes.label: Additional organelles — mitochondria, ribosomes and cell specialisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the roles of mitochondria and ribosomes as organelles present in both cell types, and recognise that cells are specialised — different cells have different organelle complements.
criteria: States the function of mitochondria and ribosomes
Explains why a named specialised cell has more or fewer of a particular organelle
Describes cell specialisation as variation in organelle complement reflecting cell function

descriptors.title: Structure, function and organ systems
descriptors.description: analyse the relationship between structure and function of cells, tissues and organs in a plant and an animal organ system and explain how these systems enable survival of the individual

nodes.label: Cell specialisation — same DNA, different structure and function
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how cells with the same genetic information become specialised for different functions, and describe structural features of two or more specialised cell types.
criteria: Describes at least two structural features of a specialised cell and explains how each serves the cell's function
Explains that cells with the same DNA can be specialised for different functions
Connects organelle complement to cell specialisation for at least one cell type

nodes.label: Tissues — groups of specialised cells performing a shared function
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define a tissue as a group of similar specialised cells performing a shared function, and give examples from plant and animal systems.
criteria: Defines a tissue as a group of similar specialised cells performing a shared function
Names at least one animal and one plant tissue with the function of each
Explains how tissue function emerges from the collective action of its component cells

nodes.label: Organs — tissues working together for an integrated function
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe an organ as a structure composed of multiple tissue types, each contributing to the organ's overall function.
criteria: Names at least two tissue types in a named organ and explains the contribution of each
Explains why organs require multiple tissue types
Analyses how a tissue-level change affects organ function

nodes.label: Organ systems — coordinated organs enabling survival
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how organs within a system coordinate to perform a survival function, applying this to one animal and one plant system.
criteria: Names the organs of one animal and one plant system and explains the function of each
Explains how the coordinated system enables a specific survival function
Compares one plant and one animal system as solutions to a shared survival problem

descriptors.title: Plate tectonics
descriptors.description: investigate tectonic activity including the formation of geological features at divergent, convergent and transform plate boundaries and describe the scientific evidence for the theory of plate tectonics

nodes.label: Earth's internal structure — layers, states and the lithosphere
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe Earth's layered internal structure, identify the state and composition of each layer, and explain that the lithosphere is the rigid outer layer.
criteria: Names Earth's main internal layers and describes the state (solid/liquid) of each
Explains that the lithosphere is the rigid outer layer (crust + upper mantle)
States that temperature and pressure increase with depth

nodes.label: Tectonic plates and the driving mechanism
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that the lithosphere is divided into tectonic plates and describe mantle convection as the mechanism driving plate movement.
criteria: Explains that the lithosphere is divided into tectonic plates that move
Describes mantle convection as the mechanism driving plate movement
States that plates move at rates of centimetres per year

nodes.label: Divergent boundaries — plates moving apart
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the geological features formed where plates diverge and explain the process producing each.
criteria: Explains that diverging plates produce tension and allow magma to rise
Describes mid-ocean ridges and seafloor spreading as products of divergent boundaries
States that oceanic crust is youngest at ridges and ages with distance

nodes.label: Convergent boundaries — plates colliding
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the geological features formed at convergent boundaries and distinguish ocean-continent from continent-continent convergence.
criteria: Describes subduction as the process at ocean-continent convergent boundaries
Explains the formation of ocean trenches and volcanic arcs at ocean-continent boundaries
Explains why continent-continent convergence produces mountain ranges rather than subduction

nodes.label: Transform boundaries — plates sliding past each other
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe transform boundaries, explain the geological features they produce, and explain why earthquakes are concentrated there.
criteria: Describes transform boundaries as plates sliding horizontally past each other
Explains why earthquakes occur at transform boundaries (stress build-up and release)
States that transform boundaries produce earthquakes but not volcanic activity

nodes.label: Evidence for plate tectonics — multiple converging lines
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe at least three independent lines of evidence supporting the theory of plate tectonics and explain what each demonstrates.
criteria: Describes at least three distinct lines of evidence supporting plate tectonics
Explains what each evidence type demonstrates about plate movement or history
Identifies seafloor age patterns as particularly strong evidence for seafloor spreading

descriptors.title: Rock cycle
descriptors.description: describe the key processes of the rock cycle, including the timescales over which they occur, and examine how the properties of sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic rocks reflect their formation and influence their use

nodes.label: Sedimentary rocks — weathering, transport, deposition and lithification
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the formation of sedimentary rocks through the sequence of weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition and lithification, and connect observable properties to formation.
criteria: Describes the formation sequence: weathering → erosion → transport → deposition → lithification
Connects at least two observable properties of sedimentary rock to formation steps
Identifies fossils as occurring in sedimentary rocks and explains why

nodes.label: Igneous rocks — magma cooling and crystallisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the formation of igneous rocks from cooling magma or lava and connect crystal size to cooling rate.
criteria: Distinguishes intrusive (underground, slow cooling) from extrusive (surface, rapid cooling) igneous formation
Explains that slower cooling produces larger crystals
Applies cooling rate reasoning to infer the formation environment of a named igneous rock

nodes.label: Metamorphic rocks — heat and pressure without melting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain metamorphic rock formation through heat and pressure applied to existing rock, and describe observable properties that reflect these conditions.
criteria: Explains that metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are subjected to heat and pressure without melting
Connects banding or foliation to the directional compression of metamorphism
Identifies at least one parent rock and its metamorphic product

nodes.label: The rock cycle — processes connecting all three types over geological time
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the rock cycle as a set of interconnected processes by which rocks are continuously transformed between types, and identify the geological timescales involved.
criteria: Traces at least two complete rock cycle pathways, naming the process at each step
Compares the timescales of surface and deep rock cycle processes
Explains how plate tectonics drives the rock cycle

nodes.label: Rock properties, formation history and use
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the properties of each rock type reflect its formation history and evaluate the suitability of specific rocks for named uses.
criteria: Explains the properties of at least two rock types in terms of their formation processes
Connects named rock properties to suitability for a specific use
Identifies how traditional rock selection practices reflect knowledge of formation-linked properties

descriptors.title: Energy transfer and transformation
descriptors.description: classify different types of energy as kinetic or potential and investigate energy transfer and transformations in simple systems

nodes.label: Kinetic energy — energy of active processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify kinetic energy types, explain what they share in common, and classify familiar examples.
criteria: Names at least four kinetic energy types
Explains the shared characteristic of kinetic energy forms (associated with activity or motion)
Correctly classifies novel energy examples as kinetic

nodes.label: Potential energy — stored capacity for activity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify potential energy types, explain the stored-capacity principle, and classify familiar examples.
criteria: Names at least three potential energy types
Explains potential energy as stored capacity — not currently active
Distinguishes potential from kinetic energy and identifies the condition that determines each

nodes.label: Energy transfer — same type, different location
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define energy transfer as energy moving between objects without changing type, and give examples of thermal, mechanical and electrical transfer.
criteria: Defines energy transfer as energy moving between objects without changing type
Gives two examples of energy transfer involving different energy types
Distinguishes a transfer event from a transformation event

nodes.label: Energy transformation — energy changing type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define energy transformation as energy changing from one type to another, identify common transformation sequences, and explain by-product heat.
criteria: Defines energy transformation as energy changing from one type to another
Identifies useful output and by-product heat in at least two named transformations
Explains that by-product heat is not lost (energy is conserved) but is not the useful output

nodes.label: Tracing energy through multi-step systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can trace energy through a multi-step system, naming the energy type at each stage and identifying all transfers, transformations and by-product outputs.
criteria: Traces energy through a multi-step system naming all types at each stage
Identifies all transfers, transformations and by-product outputs in the trace
Distinguishes useful energy output from by-product outputs

nodes.label: Flow diagrams — representing and analysing energy systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct and interpret flow diagrams representing energy through a system and use these to identify where by-product outputs occur.
criteria: Constructs a flow diagram for a multi-step system with correctly labelled energy types
Includes by-product outputs at each transformation stage
Critiques a diagram for completeness — identifies any missing outputs

descriptors.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
descriptors.description: classify matter as elements, compounds or mixtures and compare different representations of these, including 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional models, symbols for elements and formulas for molecules and compounds

nodes.label: Atoms and atom types — giving the particle model identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that particles in the particle model are atoms, that atoms have type (element identity), and that different substances are made of different atom types.
criteria: Explains that the particles in the particle model are atoms
States that different elements consist of different types of atoms
Explains that atom type determines element identity

nodes.label: Elements — one atom type, symbols and the periodic table
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define elements as pure substances consisting of only one type of atom and use chemical symbols to represent them.
criteria: Defines an element as a pure substance consisting of only one type of atom
Correctly uses symbols for at least five elements
Uses the periodic table to locate element symbols and names

nodes.label: Compounds — different atom types chemically combined
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define compounds as substances containing two or more atom types chemically combined in fixed ratios, and use formulas to represent them.
criteria: Defines a compound as two or more atom types chemically combined in fixed ratios
Interprets a chemical formula to identify atom types and their ratios
Explains that compounds have different properties from their constituent elements

nodes.label: Mixtures — substances physically combined, properties retained
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define mixtures, explain that components retain their properties and can be separated by physical means, and distinguish mixtures from compounds.
criteria: Defines a mixture and gives examples of solutions, suspensions and colloids
Explains that mixture components retain their individual properties
Identifies at least two differences between a mixture and a compound

nodes.label: Representations — comparing symbols, formulas and 2D/3D models
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare representations of elements, compounds and mixtures and explain what information each representation conveys and where each is most useful.
criteria: Identifies what information a symbol, formula and 3D model each convey for a named substance
Explains one advantage and one limitation of each representation type
Selects the most appropriate representation for a given purpose and justifies the choice

descriptors.title: Physical and chemical changes
descriptors.description: compare physical and chemical changes and identify indicators of energy change in chemical reactions

nodes.label: Physical change at the particle level — rearrangement without new substance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain physical change as rearrangement of particles without formation of new substances, and represent this using the particle model.
criteria: Explains physical change as particle rearrangement without formation of new substances
Represents a physical change using a particle diagram showing no new substance
