Explains why reversibility is a consequence of physical change, not the definition

nodes.label: Chemical change — new substance formation at the particle level
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain chemical change as the formation of new substances through bond breaking and forming, and apply the new substance criterion to classify changes.
criteria: States that new substance formation is the criterion defining chemical change
Correctly classifies at least three changes using the new substance criterion
Explains why reversibility alone is not a reliable criterion using a named counterexample

nodes.label: Observable indicators of chemical change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain four observable indicators of chemical change and explain why each suggests a new substance has formed.
criteria: Names four observable indicators of chemical change
Explains why each indicator suggests a new substance has formed
Distinguishes indicators (observable evidence) from the definition (new substance)

nodes.label: Exothermic reactions — energy released to surroundings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify exothermic reactions by temperature rise, explain that energy is released as bonds form in the products, and give examples.
criteria: Identifies exothermic reactions by a temperature rise in the surroundings
Explains that exothermic reactions release energy stored in chemical bonds
Gives at least two examples of exothermic reactions

nodes.label: Endothermic reactions — energy absorbed from surroundings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify endothermic reactions by temperature drop, explain that energy is absorbed to break reactant bonds, and give examples.
criteria: Identifies endothermic reactions by a temperature fall in the surroundings
Explains that endothermic reactions absorb energy from surroundings
Gives at least two examples of endothermic reactions and distinguishes them from exothermic

nodes.label: Comparing physical and chemical changes — integrating all criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply the new substance criterion, observable indicators and energy change together to classify and analyse unfamiliar changes.
criteria: Applies the new substance criterion, observable indicators and energy change to classify an unfamiliar change
Explains why multiple converging criteria increase classification confidence
Identifies a case where a single indicator is misleading and explains using the new substance criterion

descriptors.title: Peer review validates scientific knowledge
descriptors.description: explain how scientific knowledge is validated and refined, including the role of publication and peer review

nodes.label: From evidence to accepted knowledge: the validation problem
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why scientific claims require validation beyond the individual scientist — identifying that bias, error and limited evidence are reasons the scientific community needs mechanisms for checking claims.
criteria: Can state at least one reason why a single scientist's findings require external validation.
Can explain that validation processes exist to reduce errors and build reliable knowledge — not just to follow rules.
Does not treat peer review as 'just getting someone else to read it' — understands its epistemically protective function.

nodes.label: The publication and peer review process
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the publication and peer review process, including how editors evaluate submitted papers, what reviewers assess, and how the process results in validation, revision or rejection.
criteria: Can describe the key steps of peer review — not just name it.
Can explain that peer review can result in revision or rejection, not just acceptance.
Can describe what reviewers are assessing — methodology, evidence, conclusions — not just 'whether it's good'.

nodes.label: Knowledge refined: rejection and revision cases
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine cases where scientific knowledge was initially rejected, revised or debated before being accepted, and explain what role evidence played in the eventual outcome.
criteria: Can describe a case where scientific knowledge was refined and explain what evidence drove the change.
Can explain that validation is not a single event — knowledge builds through accumulation of consistent evidence.
Does not describe initial rejection as simply 'scientists being wrong' — explains the epistemic reasons for caution.

descriptors.title: Science and technology advance together
descriptors.description: investigate how advances in technologies enable advances in science, and how science has contributed to developments in technologies and engineering

nodes.label: Technology enabling science
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe cases where advances in technology enabled advances in scientific understanding — explaining what the technology made possible that was not possible before.
criteria: Can describe at least one example where technology enabled a scientific advance.
Can explain what the technology specifically made possible — not just that 'it helped'.
Does not treat the relationship as simply 'scientists use tools' — understands that the tool opened a previously inaccessible domain.

nodes.label: Science enabling technology
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe cases where scientific understanding enabled the development of new technologies or engineering solutions — explaining how the science provided the theoretical foundation for the technology.
criteria: Can describe at least one example where scientific understanding enabled a technological development.
Can explain the specific connection — what understanding made the technology possible.
Does not treat science and technology as sequential ('science first, then technology') — can recognise cases of mutual enablement.

nodes.label: The two-way relationship
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate the two-directional relationship between science and technology — recognising that the relationship is iterative, not sequential, and can examine multiple cases where each has enabled the other in a cycle of development.
criteria: Can explain what 'two-directional' means in the science-technology relationship — not just state it.
Can provide an example where both directions are visible — technology enabling science AND science enabling technology in the same domain.
Does not treat the relationship as sequential — understands it as iterative and ongoing.

descriptors.title: Factors in science adoption
descriptors.description: analyse the key factors that contribute to science knowledge and practices being adopted more broadly by society

nodes.label: Adoption factors: the concept
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that scientific knowledge being valid or published is not sufficient for broad societal adoption, and identify the types of factors that affect whether adoption occurs.
criteria: Can explain why scientific validity alone is insufficient for societal adoption.
Can identify at least two distinct categories of adoption factors.
Does not treat 'getting the word out' as the only obstacle — recognises structural, economic and cultural factors.

nodes.label: Analysing adoption cases
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse specific cases of scientific knowledge or practice adoption, identifying the key factors that contributed to or inhibited adoption in each case.
criteria: Can identify at least two adoption factors in a named case and explain how each operated.
Can explain whether adoption was rapid or slow and connect this to the factor profile.
Does not simply describe what was adopted — analyses the conditions that made adoption possible.

descriptors.title: Society shapes scientific research
descriptors.description: examine how the values and needs of society influence the focus of scientific research

nodes.label: Who decides what gets researched?
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that scientific research requires funding and that decisions about what research is funded reflect societal values and priorities — introducing the concept that research focus is not determined by science alone.
criteria: Can explain that research requires funding and that funding decisions reflect priorities.
Can identify at least one way societal values influence research direction.
Does not treat research focus as determined by scientific curiosity alone — understands external shaping.

nodes.label: Examining cases of society-driven research
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine specific cases where the values and needs of society have influenced the focus of scientific research — identifying the societal driver and the resulting research direction.
criteria: Can identify the societal need or value that drove a named research direction.
Can explain the connection — not just list the case but trace the pathway from value/need to research priority.
Does not treat all research as societally driven in the same way — can distinguish government mandate, market incentive, community need and cultural value as distinct mechanisms.

descriptors.title: Investigable questions, predictions and hypotheses
descriptors.description: develop investigable questions, reasoned predictions and hypotheses to test relationships and develop explanatory models

nodes.label: What makes a question investigable?
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish investigable from non-investigable questions, and explain the criteria that make a scientific question investigable — including that it must be answerable through observable, measurable evidence.
criteria: Can identify whether a question is investigable and explain why or why not.
Can improve a vague question by making it specific about variables.
Does not treat 'interesting' as a criterion for investigability — uses testability.

nodes.label: Reasoned predictions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a reasoned prediction that states an expected outcome and provides a reason based on scientific knowledge — not just a guess.
criteria: Can write a prediction that includes both an expected outcome and a scientific reason.
Can distinguish a reasoned prediction from a guess — the reason is grounded in science, not preference.
Does not omit the reason — treats the because-clause as mandatory.

nodes.label: Hypotheses: testable, refutable, relationship-specifying
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a formal hypothesis that specifies the predicted relationship between variables in a form that can be supported or refuted through evidence, and explain why scientific hypotheses must be refutable.
criteria: Can write a hypothesis that specifies the relationship between named variables.
Can identify what result would refute their hypothesis.
Does not write vague or circular hypotheses — the prediction must be specific enough to test.

descriptors.title: Plan valid, reproducible investigations
descriptors.description: plan and conduct valid, reproducible investigations to answer questions and test hypotheses, including identifying and controlling for possible sources of error and, as appropriate, developing and following risk assessments, considering ethical issues, and addressing key considerations regarding heritage sites and artefacts on Country/Place

nodes.label: Validity and reproducibility as method criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what validity and reproducibility mean as criteria for a scientific investigation method, and identify whether a described method satisfies each criterion.
criteria: Can define validity and reproducibility with precision — not just 'it works' and 'you can do it again'.
Can identify a specific feature of a method that threatens validity or reproducibility.
Does not conflate the two criteria — can explain how a method could be reproducible but not valid.

nodes.label: Identifying and controlling sources of error
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify possible sources of error in an investigation method and explain how controlling or accounting for each error source increases validity and reproducibility.
criteria: Can identify at least two sources of error with specific explanations — not generic 'human error'.
Can describe a specific control strategy for each identified error source.
Can explain how uncontrolled error affects the validity of conclusions.

nodes.label: Risk assessment, ethics and Country/Place considerations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify potential hazards in an investigation, develop a risk assessment, consider ethical issues relevant to the investigation context, and describe responsibilities regarding heritage sites and artefacts on Country/Place.
criteria: Can identify at least one investigation hazard and describe a control measure.
Can identify at least one ethical consideration relevant to a described investigation.
Can describe responsibilities regarding heritage sites in field investigation contexts.

descriptors.title: Select equipment and record precise data
descriptors.description: select and use equipment to generate and record data with precision to obtain useful sample sizes and replicable data, using digital tools as appropriate

nodes.label: Precision in measurement and recording
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what precision means in measurement, select equipment based on required precision, and record data values to the correct number of significant figures with appropriate units.
criteria: Can select between two instruments based on required precision and explain the choice.
Can record data to the correct number of significant figures for the instrument used.
Does not record more significant figures than the instrument can provide.

nodes.label: Sample size and replicability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why sample size matters for the quality of scientific data and justify a sample size choice for a described investigation context — considering what constitutes a useful sample size.
criteria: Can explain why sample size affects reliability of results.
Can identify the relevant factors for determining appropriate sample size in a described investigation.
Does not default to 'more is always better' without considering practical constraints and the specific investigation context.

descriptors.title: Select and construct appropriate representations
descriptors.description: select and construct appropriate representations, including tables, graphs, descriptive statistics, models and mathematical relationships, to organise and process data and information

nodes.label: Selecting appropriate representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select the most appropriate representation for a given data type or investigation question and explain the rationale for their choice.
criteria: Can select an appropriate representation and explain the rationale — not just produce the representation.
Can identify when an alternative representation would be less appropriate and explain why.
Does not default to a single graph type for all data.

nodes.label: Descriptive statistics: selecting the appropriate measure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the most appropriate descriptive statistic (mean, median or range) for a given data set and explain why — recognising that mean and median can differ and that each is appropriate in different contexts.
criteria: Can calculate mean, median and range for a small data set.
Can identify which measure is most appropriate for a described data type and explain why.
Does not default to mean for all data without considering whether it is appropriate.

nodes.label: Constructing and using mathematical relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply mathematical relationships (formulae, ratios, proportional reasoning) to process data, and construct representations that accurately reflect quantitative relationships.
criteria: Can apply a given formula correctly to process data.
Can construct a representation where numerical values determine proportional layout (e.g. Sankey diagram).
Can explain what the processed representation reveals that raw data does not.

descriptors.title: Analyse data for patterns and anomalies
descriptors.description: analyse and connect a variety of data and information to identify and explain patterns, trends, relationships and anomalies

nodes.label: Identifying patterns, trends and relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify patterns (repeating features), trends (directional change over a variable) and relationships (one variable changing in response to another) in data sets, using appropriate descriptive language.
criteria: Can describe a pattern or trend naming both variables and the direction of change.
Can distinguish between a trend (directional change), a pattern (repeating feature) and a relationship (covariance).
Does not use vague language like 'it goes up' — uses the variable names.

nodes.label: Identifying and explaining anomalies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify anomalies in data — data points that do not fit the identified pattern — and propose explanations for them in terms of measurement error, procedural variation or genuine outliers.
criteria: Can identify an anomalous data point as one that does not fit the identified pattern.
Can propose a plausible explanation for an anomaly that distinguishes between error and genuine variation.
Does not treat all anomalies the same — can evaluate whether an anomaly should be excluded or investigated.

nodes.label: Connecting and comparing data sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can connect and compare data from multiple sources to identify consistencies, inconsistencies and what they mean for scientific claims — including discussing the validity of extrapolation from data.
criteria: Can identify consistency and inconsistency across two data sources on the same topic.
Can explain what an inconsistency implies for confidence in a conclusion.
Can discuss the validity of an extrapolation — identifying the assumption it requires.

descriptors.title: Assess validity and evaluate conclusions
descriptors.description: assess the validity and reproducibility of methods and evaluate the validity of conclusions and claims, including by identifying assumptions, conflicting evidence and areas of uncertainty

nodes.label: Validity of secondary source information
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what makes secondary source information valid and evaluate a secondary source against validity criteria — distinguishing credible from less credible sources.
criteria: Can apply at least two validity criteria to evaluate a named secondary source.
Can identify specific features of the source that support or undermine its credibility.
Does not treat all published sources as equally valid.

nodes.label: Identifying assumptions in methods and conclusions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify assumptions embedded in investigation methods and conclusions, and evaluate the impact of these assumptions on the validity of conclusions.
criteria: Can identify at least one assumption in a described method or conclusion.
Can explain the impact of that assumption being false on conclusion validity.
Does not treat methods as assumption-free — recognises that all methods contain assumptions.

nodes.label: Conflicting evidence and areas of uncertainty
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify conflicting evidence within or across investigations and explain how areas of uncertainty may support viable alternative conclusions.
criteria: Can identify an area of uncertainty or conflicting evidence in a described investigation.
Can explain how that uncertainty or evidence could support an alternative conclusion.
Does not treat all uncertainty as equally undermining — can evaluate the significance of identified uncertainty.

descriptors.title: Construct evidence-based arguments ethically
descriptors.description: construct arguments based on analysis of a variety of evidence to support conclusions or evaluate claims, and consider any ethical issues and cultural protocols associated with accessing, using or citing secondary data or information

nodes.label: Constructing multi-source arguments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct an argument that draws on multiple sources of evidence, evaluating the credibility of each source and explaining how the evidence collectively supports the conclusion.
criteria: Can construct an argument using at least two sources with explicit credibility evaluation.
Can explain how the evidence collectively supports the conclusion — not just list the sources.
Does not construct an argument from a single source — uses multiple independent sources.

nodes.label: Ethical issues in secondary data use
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify ethical issues associated with accessing, using and citing secondary data — including data privacy, correct attribution, and relevance to the investigation question.
criteria: Can identify at least one ethical concern in a described secondary data use scenario.
Can describe a practice that addresses the identified concern.
Does not treat ethics in data use as purely about plagiarism — recognises privacy and relevance as separate concerns.

nodes.label: Cultural protocols with First Nations knowledges
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply cultural protocols when accessing, using or citing First Nations knowledges — including acknowledging the co-contributions of Indigenous knowledge and contemporary science, and constructing arguments that recognise these relationships appropriately.
criteria: Can describe at least one cultural protocol relevant to using First Nations knowledge in a scientific argument.
Can construct an argument that appropriately acknowledges First Nations knowledge contributions.
Does not treat First Nations knowledge as merely contextual decoration — can use it as substantive evidence.

descriptors.title: Communicate ideas and findings effectively
descriptors.description: write and create texts to communicate ideas, findings and arguments effectively for identified purposes and audiences, including selection of appropriate content, language and text features, using digital tools as appropriate

nodes.label: Purpose, audience and communication choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse scientific texts for different purposes and audiences and explain how the author's choices — of content, language and text features — reflect the purpose and audience.
criteria: Can identify at least two communication choices in a text and connect each to the text's purpose or audience.
Can explain why different purposes or audiences require different content, language or structure.
Does not treat scientific communication as one-size-fits-all.

nodes.label: Writing a scientific investigation report
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a scientific investigation report that includes: a background paragraph referencing relevant scientific knowledge; an explanation of results using scientific knowledge; and a discussion that considers validity and reproducibility.
criteria: Can write a background paragraph that references relevant scientific knowledge — not just describes the procedure.
Can explain results using scientific knowledge — not just state what happened.
Can write a validity/reproducibility discussion that addresses specific features of the method — not just 'it could have been more accurate'.

nodes.label: Communicating for non-specialist audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create texts for non-specialist purposes and audiences — including selecting appropriate content, language and cultural sensitivity — such as social media campaigns, community reports or public presentations.
criteria: Can produce a text that is appropriate for the specified audience and purpose — as assessed against the communication choices made, not just the content.
Can adjust language from scientific register to audience-appropriate register deliberately — not just simplify randomly.
Can identify where cultural responsiveness considerations have shaped content or language choices.

descriptors.title: Body systems and negative feedback
descriptors.description: compare the role of body systems in regulating and coordinating the body's response to a stimulus, and describe the operation of a negative feedback mechanism

nodes.label: Stimuli and receptors — detecting change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish internal from external stimuli and identify the receptor type involved in detecting a named stimulus.
criteria: Distinguishes internal from external stimuli with examples
Identifies an appropriate receptor for a named stimulus and describes its role

nodes.label: Receptor → command centre → effector pathway
nodes.checkpoint: Students can trace the receptor → command centre → effector pathway for a named stimulus, describing the role of each component.
criteria: Traces the receptor → command centre → effector pathway for a named stimulus
Describes the distinct role of each component in the response

nodes.label: Nervous and endocrine systems as coordination mechanisms — signal types and timescales
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how the nervous and endocrine systems each implement the receptor → command centre → effector pathway, distinguishing signal type, speed, and duration.
criteria: Describes the nervous system pathway for a named stimulus, identifying electrical signalling and fast, short response
Describes the endocrine system pathway for a named stimulus, identifying hormonal signalling, bloodstream transport, and slower, sustained response

nodes.label: Comparing nervous and endocrine coordination
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the nervous and endocrine systems on signal type, speed, duration, and specificity, and predict which system coordinates a given stimulus.
criteria: Compares the nervous and endocrine systems on signal type, speed, and duration
Predicts which system coordinates a given novel stimulus and justifies the prediction

nodes.label: Negative feedback architecture — set point, deviation, corrective response, return detection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the four components of a negative feedback mechanism and explain why it maintains stability rather than amplifying change.
criteria: Labels and describes the role of each of the four components of a negative feedback loop
Explains why the mechanism is described as 'negative' — it opposes rather than amplifies deviation

nodes.label: Negative feedback in canonical biological cases — tracing complete loops
nodes.checkpoint: Students can trace a complete negative feedback loop for at least two named biological examples, correctly identifying all four components in each.
criteria: Traces a complete negative feedback loop for a named biological example, correctly identifying all four components
Names at least two biological examples of negative feedback and identifies the set point in each

nodes.label: Feedback system disorders — locating failure in the loop
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how a disorder of a feedback system disrupts homeostasis by identifying which component of the loop has failed and describing the consequence.
criteria: Identifies which component of the feedback loop fails in a named disorder
Explains the homeostatic consequence of that failure

descriptors.title: Reproduction and species survival
descriptors.description: describe the form and function of reproductive cells and organs in animals and plants, and analyse how the processes of sexual and asexual reproduction enable survival of the species

nodes.label: Reproductive cells — form matched to function
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the structural features of male and female gametes and explain how each feature relates to the gamete's reproductive function.
criteria: Describes at least two structural features of sperm and two of egg cells
Explains how each feature relates to the gamete's function
Identifies plant equivalents (pollen, ovule) and describes one form-function relationship in each

nodes.label: Reproductive organs — systems supporting gamete production and fertilisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the key structures of male and female reproductive systems in animals and plants and explain how these work collectively to support gamete production, transfer and fertilisation.
criteria: Names key structures of animal reproductive systems and explains the role of each
Describes plant reproductive structures (stamen, carpel) and their roles in pollination and fertilisation
Explains how reproductive organ structures collectively support fertilisation

nodes.label: Sexual reproduction — fertilisation, variation and survival
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how sexual reproduction produces variation among offspring and analyse how this variation supports species survival.
criteria: Explains how random combination of gametes produces genetic variation among offspring
Connects variation to survival advantage — some offspring are more likely to survive changed conditions
Explains the trade-off between offspring number, parental care and reproductive strategy in a named example

nodes.label: Asexual reproduction — strategies, speed and survival contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe asexual reproductive strategies in plants and animals and explain when asexual reproduction is advantageous for species survival.
criteria: Describes at least two distinct asexual reproductive strategies with examples
Explains why asexual reproduction is advantageous in stable environments or for rapid colonisation
Identifies the key limitation of asexual reproduction — genetic uniformity and vulnerability to change

nodes.label: Comparing reproductive strategies — analysing survival trade-offs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare sexual and asexual reproduction and analyse how each strategy enables species survival in different environmental contexts.
criteria: Compares sexual and asexual reproduction across variation, speed and resource cost
Analyses the survival advantage of each strategy in a specific named environmental context
Explains why some species use both strategies depending on conditions

descriptors.title: Carbon cycle and Earth's spheres
descriptors.description: represent the carbon cycle and examine how key processes including combustion, photosynthesis and respiration rely on interactions between Earth's spheres (the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere)

nodes.label: Earth's spheres — geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name and describe Earth's four spheres and give examples of matter or processes found in each.
criteria: Names all four of Earth's spheres and describes what each contains
Gives at least one example of matter and one process located in each sphere
Explains that Earth functions as a system where spheres interact

nodes.label: Carbon as a substance cycling through Earth's spheres
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify where carbon is stored in each of Earth's spheres and explain that carbon moves between these stores.
criteria: Identifies carbon stores in at least three of Earth's four spheres with examples
Explains that carbon moves between stores rather than being created or destroyed
Distinguishes fast-cycling carbon stores (atmosphere, living organisms) from slow stores (fossil fuels, carbonate rock)

nodes.label: Photosynthesis and respiration — carbon movement through the biosphere
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how photosynthesis and respiration move carbon between the atmosphere and biosphere, and represent these as flows in the carbon cycle.
criteria: Explains that photosynthesis moves carbon from the atmosphere to the biosphere
Explains that respiration and decomposition move carbon from the biosphere to the atmosphere
Represents both processes as directional arrows between spheres in a diagram

nodes.label: Combustion — carbon release from geosphere to atmosphere
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how combustion of fossil fuels moves carbon from the geosphere to the atmosphere and describe the impact of human activity on this flow.
criteria: Explains that combustion of fossil fuels moves carbon from geosphere to atmosphere
Describes why this represents a net addition to the atmospheric carbon store (geological timescale of sequestration vs rapid release)
Connects increased atmospheric CO₂ to the greenhouse effect and its role in heat retention

nodes.label: Representing the carbon cycle — integrating processes across all spheres
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct or annotate a carbon cycle diagram that represents all key processes (photosynthesis, respiration, combustion, decomposition) as flows between Earth's spheres.
criteria: Constructs or correctly annotates a carbon cycle diagram with at least four labelled flows between named spheres
Identifies which flows are biological, which are geological, and which are human-driven
Explains how human combustion has altered the balance of the natural carbon cycle

descriptors.title: Wave and particle models
descriptors.description: use wave and particle models to describe energy transfer through different mediums and examine the usefulness of each model for explaining phenomena

nodes.label: The particle model of energy transfer — conduction and convection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain conduction and convection using the particle model, describing how particle motion and collisions transfer energy through matter.
criteria: Explains conduction using particle collisions as the transfer mechanism
Explains convection using bulk particle movement driven by density differences
Applies the particle model to explain why a named material is a good conductor or insulator

nodes.label: The wave model of energy transfer — sound
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe sound as a wave and explain how sound energy is transferred through a medium using the wave model, including the relationship between wave properties and sound characteristics.
criteria: Describes sound as a longitudinal wave requiring a medium
Uses compression and rarefaction to explain how sound energy is transferred
Relates frequency to pitch and amplitude to loudness with examples

nodes.label: The particle model of electricity — static charge and current
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain static electricity and electrical current using the particle model of charge, and connect particle behaviour to concepts of voltage, conductors and insulators.
criteria: Explains static electricity as electron transfer between materials producing charge imbalance
Describes electrical current as directed electron flow through a conductor
Distinguishes conductors from insulators using the particle model (free vs bound electrons)

nodes.label: The wave model of light and electromagnetic radiation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe light and electromagnetic radiation as waves and explain how the wave model accounts for phenomena including reflection, refraction and the electromagnetic spectrum.
criteria: Describes light as a transverse wave and the EM spectrum as a family of waves differing in frequency and wavelength
Uses the wave model to explain reflection and refraction
Explains how wave frequency relates to energy across the electromagnetic spectrum

nodes.label: Evaluating model usefulness — wave vs particle for different phenomena
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the usefulness of wave and particle models for explaining different energy transfer phenomena and identify where each model succeeds or fails.
criteria: Evaluates the usefulness of each model for at least two distinct phenomena
Identifies at least one phenomenon where the wave model is more useful and one where the particle model is more useful
Explains that scientific models are tools with domains of usefulness rather than literal descriptions of reality

descriptors.title: Conservation of energy and efficiency
descriptors.description: apply the law of conservation of energy to analyse system efficiency in terms of energy inputs, outputs, transfers and transformations

nodes.label: Conservation of energy — total energy is maintained in any system
nodes.checkpoint: Students can state the law of conservation of energy and apply it to account for all energy in a system — including energy that is transferred as heat or sound rather than as useful output.
criteria: States the law of conservation of energy correctly
Explains that 'wasted' energy is transferred to the environment, not destroyed
Accounts for all energy outputs (useful + wasted) in a simple system

nodes.label: Efficiency — useful output as a proportion of total input
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define efficiency, calculate it as a ratio of useful output to total input energy, and explain why no real system achieves 100% efficiency.
criteria: Calculates efficiency as useful output ÷ total input with correct units
Explains why no real system achieves 100% efficiency
Compares efficiency values across two systems and interprets the difference

nodes.label: Sankey diagrams — representing energy inputs, outputs and losses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct and interpret Sankey diagrams to represent energy flow through a system, reading off efficiency and identifying where energy losses occur.
criteria: Reads efficiency and identifies major energy losses from a given Sankey diagram
Constructs a Sankey diagram from energy data with correctly proportioned arrows
Critiques a Sankey diagram — identifies what it represents well and any limitations

nodes.label: Applying conservation of energy and efficiency to real systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply the law of conservation of energy and efficiency analysis to evaluate real energy systems and identify where improvements could be made.
criteria: Applies conservation of energy to account for all energy inputs and outputs in a real system
Calculates efficiency for a real system and interprets the result
Identifies where energy losses occur and suggests a practical improvement

descriptors.title: Atomic model and radioactive decay
descriptors.description: explain how the model of the atom changed following the discovery of electrons, protons and neutrons and describe how natural radioactive decay results in stable atoms

nodes.label: The nuclear model of the atom — protons, neutrons and electrons
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the structure of the nuclear atom in terms of protons, neutrons and electrons, and use atomic number and mass number to describe specific atoms.
criteria: Describes the nuclear atom: protons and neutrons in the nucleus, electrons in shells
Uses atomic number and mass number to determine proton, neutron and electron counts
Describes the relative mass and charge of protons, neutrons and electrons

nodes.label: Isotopes — same element, different neutron numbers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define isotopes as atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, and explain why some isotopes are unstable.
criteria: Defines isotopes as atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
Identifies that some isotopes are unstable and undergo radioactive decay
Uses isotope notation (e.g. carbon-14) correctly

nodes.label: Types of radioactive decay — alpha, beta and gamma
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe alpha, beta and gamma decay in terms of what is emitted and how each changes the nucleus, and compare their penetrating power.
criteria: Describes what is emitted in alpha, beta and gamma decay
Explains how alpha and beta decay change the atomic number and mass number of the nucleus
Compares the penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation

nodes.label: Half-life — rate of radioactive decay
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define half-life, use half-life data to calculate remaining activity after a given number of half-lives, and explain how half-life determines the suitability of isotopes for different applications.
criteria: Defines half-life as the time for half of the nuclei in a sample to decay
Calculates the remaining quantity of a radioisotope after a given number of half-lives
Explains why half-life determines the suitability of an isotope for a named application

nodes.label: Decay sequences — how unstable isotopes reach stability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how a series of decay events transforms an unstable isotope into a stable one, and explain the relationship between the descriptor's descriptor claim that 'natural radioactive decay results in stable atoms'.
criteria: Traces a named decay sequence and identifies the stable end product
Tracks changes to atomic number and mass number at each decay step
Explains how the sequence of decay events moves the nucleus toward stability

descriptors.title: Chemical equations and conservation of mass
descriptors.description: model the rearrangement of atoms in chemical reactions using a range of representations, including word and simple balanced chemical equations, and use these to demonstrate the law of conservation of mass

nodes.label: Reactants and products — identifying what changes in a chemical reaction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify reactants and products in a chemical reaction and describe the change in terms of new substances being formed.
criteria: Identifies reactants and products in a named chemical reaction
Explains that chemical reactions produce new substances with different properties
Connects reactant-product change to prior indicators of chemical change (AC9S8U07)

nodes.label: Atom rearrangement — chemical reactions as atomic-level redistribution
nodes.checkpoint: Students can model a chemical reaction as the rearrangement of atoms using molecular models or diagrams, showing that atoms are neither created nor destroyed.
criteria: Uses a molecular model or diagram to represent a simple reaction showing atoms before and after
Counts atoms on each side of a representation and confirms they match
Explains that atoms are rearranged — not created or destroyed — in chemical reactions

nodes.label: Word equations — naming reactants and products
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write correct word equations for named chemical reactions, correctly identifying all reactants and products.
criteria: Writes a correct word equation for at least two named reactions, including all products
Uses correct arrow notation (reactants → products)
Explains what word equations show and what they do not (no quantities, no atom counts)

nodes.label: Balanced symbolic equations — demonstrating conservation of mass
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write and balance simple symbolic chemical equations and explain why balancing demonstrates the law of conservation of mass.
criteria: Balances a simple symbolic equation by adjusting coefficients (not subscripts)
Verifies a balanced equation by counting atoms of each element on both sides
Explains that a balanced equation demonstrates conservation of mass — same atoms, same total mass, on both sides

nodes.label: Conservation of mass — connecting representation to empirical evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use balanced equations to explain the law of conservation of mass, and connect this to experimental evidence from reactions in closed and open systems.
criteria: Explains why total mass is conserved in a closed system chemical reaction
Explains apparent mass changes in open system reactions using conservation of mass
Uses a balanced equation to connect the symbolic representation to the empirical mass conservation result

descriptors.title: Genetics and inheritance
descriptors.description: explain the role of meiosis and mitosis and the function of chromosomes, DNA and genes in heredity and predict patterns of Mendelian inheritance

nodes.label: Chromosomes, DNA and genes — the structural hierarchy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the structural relationship between chromosomes, DNA and genes, and explain how genetic information is organised and stored.
criteria: Describes chromosomes as structures made of DNA
Explains that genes are segments of DNA that code for heritable characteristics
Distinguishes genotype (genetic information) from phenotype (expressed characteristic)

nodes.label: Mitosis — cell division for growth and repair
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the outcome of mitosis and describe its role in growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
criteria: States that mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells
Explains that chromosome number is maintained through mitosis
Identifies growth and repair as the biological purposes of mitosis

nodes.label: Meiosis — halving chromosome number and generating variation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how meiosis halves the chromosome number to produce gametes and describe how meiosis generates genetic variation.
criteria: Explains that meiosis halves the chromosome number to produce gametes
Describes that each gamete receives one chromosome from each homologous pair
Explains how meiosis contributes to genetic variation in offspring

nodes.label: Alleles and Mendelian inheritance — dominant and recessive
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain dominant and recessive allele relationships and use Punnett squares to predict genotype and phenotype ratios in monohybrid crosses.
criteria: Constructs a Punnett square for a monohybrid cross and states correct genotype and phenotype ratios
Uses correct allele notation and correctly forms gametes from each parental genotype
Interprets a pedigree diagram to identify phenotypes and infer genotypes for dominant/recessive traits

nodes.label: Fertilisation and heredity — connecting meiosis to offspring variation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how meiosis and fertilisation together determine heredity and account for variation among siblings from the same parents.
criteria: Traces the pathway from parent genotypes through meiosis, gametes and fertilisation to offspring genotype
Explains why siblings from the same parents can have different genotypes and phenotypes
Connects Punnett square probability ratios to the random combination of gametes at fertilisation

nodes.label: Sex-linked inheritance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain sex determination by sex chromosomes and predict genotype and phenotype ratios for sex-linked traits using Punnett squares.
criteria: Explains that sex is determined by the X and Y chromosome pair
Uses correct X-linked allele notation in a Punnett square and predicts phenotype ratios for males and females
Identifies why X-linked recessive conditions are more frequently expressed in males than females

descriptors.title: Evolution by natural selection
descriptors.description: use the theory of evolution by natural selection to explain past and present diversity and analyse the scientific evidence supporting the theory

nodes.label: Variation within populations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that individuals within a population vary in heritable characteristics and identify the sources of that variation.
criteria: Explains that individuals within a population vary in heritable characteristics
Distinguishes heritable from non-heritable variation
Identifies mutation and sexual reproduction as sources of heritable variation

nodes.label: Natural selection as a mechanism — variation, selection pressure, differential survival
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the mechanism of natural selection: how a selection pressure acts on heritable variation to produce differential survival and reproduction, leading to population change over generations.
criteria: Describes the mechanism of natural selection as variation → selection pressure → differential survival/reproduction → inherited by offspring
Applies the mechanism correctly to a named example
Distinguishes natural selection from the Lamarckian view that individuals adapt during their lifetime

nodes.label: Evidence for evolution — multiple lines of support
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe and explain multiple lines of evidence that support the theory of evolution by natural selection, including the fossil record, anatomical and chemical similarities, and geographical distribution.
criteria: Describes at least three distinct lines of evidence for evolution
Explains what each evidence type demonstrates about common descent or change over time
Identifies that multiple independent evidence types support the same conclusion

nodes.label: Using natural selection to explain past diversity — speciation and extinction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the theory of natural selection to explain how past populations diverged into new species and how extinction results from failed adaptation to selection pressures.
criteria: Explains how geographic isolation and different selection pressures can lead to speciation
Uses natural selection to explain why species go extinct when selection pressures change
Connects fossil record evidence to the timeline of species appearance and disappearance

nodes.label: Using natural selection to explain present diversity and current change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the theory of natural selection to explain current patterns of biodiversity and analyse examples of evolution occurring in present populations.
criteria: Applies natural selection to explain a current example of observable population change
Explains present biodiversity as the product of ongoing evolutionary processes
Analyses how a current selection pressure is affecting a named population

descriptors.title: Big Bang theory
descriptors.description: describe how the big bang theory models the origin and evolution of the universe and analyse the supporting evidence for the theory

nodes.label: Scale and structure of the universe
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the major structural components of the universe using appropriate scale and units, and place Earth within the cosmic hierarchy.
criteria: Names the major structural components of the universe in order of scale
Uses light-years or astronomical units correctly in a distance context
Uses scientific notation to express cosmological distances or ages

nodes.label: The big bang model — origin and timeline of the universe
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the big bang theory as a model of the origin and evolution of the universe and outline the major stages from the initial singularity to the formation of stars and galaxies.
criteria: Describes the big bang as the origin of space, time and matter approximately 13.8 billion years ago
Outlines at least three major stages in the universe's evolution from the initial event to galaxy formation
Explains that the universe has been expanding and cooling since the big bang

nodes.label: Redshift and the expanding universe
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the redshift of light from distant galaxies provides evidence that the universe is expanding, and connect this to the big bang model.
criteria: Explains that redshift of light from distant galaxies indicates they are moving away from us
Connects the expanding universe (evidenced by redshift) to the big bang model
Describes Hubble's observations as a key evidential basis for the expanding universe

nodes.label: Cosmic microwave background radiation and matter proportions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how cosmic microwave background radiation and the observed proportions of matter in the universe provide independent lines of evidence supporting the big bang theory.
criteria: Describes cosmic microwave background radiation and explains what it indicates about the early universe
Explains that the proportions of matter (hydrogen, helium) in the universe are consistent with big bang predictions
Identifies CMB and matter proportions as independent lines of evidence, separate from redshift

nodes.label: Analysing the evidence base — how multiple lines support the theory
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how redshift, CMB and matter proportions together constitute a mutually supporting evidence base for the big bang theory, and explain what each line independently demonstrates.
criteria: Analyses how at least three lines of evidence independently support the big bang theory
Explains what each evidence type demonstrates and why convergence strengthens the theory
Acknowledges at least one open question or area of ongoing investigation in cosmology

descriptors.title: Global climate change
descriptors.description: use models of energy flow between the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere to explain patterns of global climate change

nodes.label: Solar radiation and Earth's energy input
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how solar radiation reaches Earth and identify the factors that determine how much energy is absorbed versus reflected by the surface and atmosphere.
criteria: Identifies the sun as the primary energy input to Earth's climate system
Distinguishes absorbed from reflected solar radiation with at least one surface example
Explains why different surfaces absorb or reflect different proportions of solar radiation

nodes.label: Energy balance between Earth's spheres
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how energy flows between the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere and explain what it means for Earth to be in energy balance.
criteria: Describes energy exchange between at least three of the four spheres
Explains energy balance as the condition where incoming and outgoing energy are equal over time
Identifies the ocean or atmosphere as a store and distributor of heat energy

nodes.label: The greenhouse effect — trapping outgoing radiation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how greenhouse gases in the atmosphere trap outgoing infrared radiation and describe the role of this mechanism in maintaining Earth's surface temperature.
criteria: Explains that Earth emits infrared radiation and that greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit it
Distinguishes natural greenhouse effect from enhanced greenhouse effect
Locates the greenhouse mechanism correctly within the energy balance model from N2 (atmosphere slows outgoing, not incoming, energy)

nodes.label: Human activity, greenhouse gas concentrations and energy imbalance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how human activities increase atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations and describe how this creates an energy imbalance that drives warming.
criteria: Identifies at least two human activities that increase atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations
Explains how increased greenhouse gas concentration leads to a positive energy imbalance
Connects the perturbation of atmospheric CO₂ to the energy flow model from N2 and N3

nodes.label: Indicators of climate change across Earth's spheres
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and interpret multiple indicators of climate change and explain each as evidence of the energy imbalance described in N4.
criteria: Names at least three distinct climate change indicators across different spheres
Explains the mechanism behind at least two indicators using the energy flow model
Interprets a climate data visualisation as evidence of energy imbalance

nodes.label: Using energy flow models to explain and evaluate responses to climate change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the energy flow model to explain patterns of global climate change and evaluate strategies designed to reduce or mitigate its effects in terms of the model.
criteria: Applies the energy flow model to explain at least two distinct patterns of global climate change
Evaluates at least one strategy to reduce climate change and one to mitigate its effects using the model
Distinguishes mitigation from adaptation and explains each in terms of the energy balance

descriptors.title: Newton's laws of motion
descriptors.description: investigate Newton's laws of motion and quantitatively analyse the relationship between force, mass and acceleration of objects

nodes.label: Force as a vector quantity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent forces as vectors with both magnitude and direction, and add or subtract forces acting along a single axis to find net force.
criteria: Represents a named force as a vector with a labelled magnitude and direction
Calculates net force for two forces acting along the same axis using a consistent sign convention
Distinguishes between contact forces (friction, normal) and non-contact forces (gravity)

nodes.label: Newton's First Law — inertia and the Aristotelian misconception
nodes.checkpoint: Students can state Newton's First Law and explain why a moving object with no net force continues at constant velocity, identifying and correcting the misconception that motion requires a continuous force.
criteria: States Newton's First Law correctly
Explains why a moving object without net force continues at constant velocity (does not slow down)
Identifies friction as the hidden force responsible for observed deceleration in everyday scenarios
Corrects the claim that 'a moving object needs a force to keep moving'

nodes.label: Acceleration as a defined vector quantity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity, calculate acceleration from velocity and time data, and represent acceleration as a vector with direction.
criteria: Defines acceleration as the rate of change of velocity with correct units (m/s²)
Calculates acceleration from velocity and time data
States the direction of acceleration and identifies it as the same direction as net force
Distinguishes acceleration from speed — identifies deceleration and direction change as forms of acceleration

nodes.label: Newton's Second Law — F = ma
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply F = ma to calculate force, mass or acceleration in single-force scenarios and explain qualitatively how changing mass or force affects acceleration.
criteria: Correctly applies F = ma to solve for force, mass or acceleration in a single-force scenario
Uses correct units (N, kg, m/s²) and maintains direction consistency
Explains qualitatively how doubling force or mass affects acceleration

nodes.label: Newton's Third Law — action-reaction pairs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify action-reaction force pairs in a scenario and explain why they do not cancel, despite being equal and opposite.
criteria: Identifies the action and reaction forces in a named scenario and states which object each acts on
Explains why action-reaction pairs do not cancel (they act on different objects)
Distinguishes Third Law pairs from balanced forces acting on the same object

nodes.label: Multi-force analysis and free body diagrams
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw a free body diagram for an object with multiple forces and calculate net force, then apply F = ma to determine acceleration.
criteria: Draws a correctly labelled free body diagram for an object with at least three forces
Calculates net force and resulting acceleration from a free body diagram
Applies the result to explain a real-world scenario (e.g. vehicle safety, sport)

nodes.label: Quantitative problem solving — integrating all three laws
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve multi-step force and motion problems that require selecting and applying Newton's laws, using mathematical representations including graphs and algebraic formulas.
criteria: Solves a multi-step problem applying at least two of Newton's laws with correct units throughout
Uses mathematical representations (graphs or algebraic formulas) to support a quantitative argument
Checks the reasonableness of a calculated answer in physical terms

nodes.label: Real-world applications — Newton's laws in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply Newton's laws to analyse motion in real-world contexts including vehicle safety, sport, and First Nations technologies, and explain design decisions in terms of force, mass and acceleration.
criteria: Applies at least two of Newton's laws to explain a design feature or technique in a real-world context
Explains a First Nations throwing technology in terms of force, time of application and resulting acceleration
Evaluates a vehicle safety feature quantitatively using Newton's Second Law

descriptors.title: Periodic table and atomic structure
descriptors.description: explain how the structure and properties of atoms relate to the organisation of the elements in the periodic table

nodes.label: Electron shell configuration and the Bohr model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw or describe the electron shell configuration of elements 1–20 using the Bohr model and explain the shell-filling rules.
criteria: Draws a correct Bohr diagram for any element 1–20
States the maximum electron capacity of the first three shells (2, 8, 8)
Identifies the number of outer-shell electrons for any element 1–20

nodes.label: Outer electrons and group properties — why elements in a group behave similarly
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why elements in the same group of the periodic table have similar chemical properties by reference to their outer electron shell configuration.
criteria: Explains that elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons
Uses outer electron configuration to explain the shared chemical properties of at least one group
Contrasts a reactive group (e.g. Group 1) with noble gases using outer electron configuration

nodes.label: Periodic trends — why properties repeat across periods
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe repeating patterns of properties across the periodic table and explain them as a consequence of repeating outer electron shell configurations.
criteria: Explains that a new period begins when electrons start filling a new shell
Describes that properties repeat across periods because outer electron configurations repeat
Interprets the position of an element in the table in terms of its electron shell configuration

nodes.label: Using atomic structure to predict and explain element properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the position of an element in the periodic table to predict its electron configuration and properties, and explain those properties in terms of atomic structure.
criteria: Predicts the outer electron configuration and likely properties of an element from its table position
Explains at least two element properties in terms of atomic structure
Uses the periodic table as a predictive tool — not just a reference — for an unfamiliar element

descriptors.title: Reaction types and rates
descriptors.description: identify patterns in synthesis, decomposition and displacement reactions and investigate the factors that affect reaction rates

nodes.label: Synthesis reactions — combining reactants to form a single product
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify synthesis reactions by their structural pattern (A + B → AB) and predict the product from given reactants.
criteria: Identifies a synthesis reaction by its structural pattern (two or more reactants → one product)
Writes a correct word equation for a named synthesis reaction
Predicts the product of a synthesis reaction from given reactants

nodes.label: Decomposition reactions — breaking a compound into simpler products
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify decomposition reactions by their structural pattern (AB → A + B) and describe conditions under which decomposition reactions occur.
criteria: Identifies a decomposition reaction by its structural pattern (one reactant → two or more products)
Describes at least one condition (heat or electrical energy) that drives a decomposition reaction
Writes a correct word equation for a named decomposition reaction

nodes.label: Displacement reactions — patterns of reactivity and product prediction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify single and double displacement reactions and use reactivity patterns to predict whether a displacement reaction will occur and what the products will be.
criteria: Identifies single and double displacement reactions from given equations
Uses an activity series to predict whether a single displacement reaction will occur
Predicts the products of a neutralisation or precipitation reaction

nodes.label: Reaction type patterns — classifying and predicting across all three types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can classify an unfamiliar chemical reaction as synthesis, decomposition or displacement and predict products, using structural patterns rather than memorisation.
criteria: Classifies an unfamiliar reaction as synthesis, decomposition or displacement using structural pattern
Predicts products for each reaction type from the pattern alone
Explains the classification reasoning rather than recalling named examples

nodes.label: Collision theory — the particle basis of reaction rates
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain reaction rate in terms of particle collision frequency and energy, and use collision theory to predict how changing conditions will affect rate.
criteria: Explains that reactions require particle collisions with energy above the activation energy threshold
Predicts that increasing collision frequency or energy increases reaction rate
Identifies at least two ways to increase collision frequency or energy

nodes.label: Rate factors — temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how each of the four rate factors affects reaction rate using collision theory, and investigate one factor experimentally.
criteria: Explains how each of the four rate factors affects reaction rate using collision theory
Distinguishes catalysts from reactants and explains why catalysts are not consumed
Designs or describes an investigation to test the effect of one rate factor
